newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian defence chief promises military reforms.
newsitem.headline: Russian defence chief promises military reforms.

text.p: Russian Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev declared war on waste on Wednesday in committing himself to a long campaign that will trim and modernise Moscow's vast but obsolescent armed forces.
After briefing Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in the Black Sea resort of Sochi, Sergeyev gave little away in the way of detail, but both men stressed the financial constraints.
But the head of the air force, in separate remarks, lifted the veil slightly by saying as much as a third of his corps would go and suggesting the cuts could be similar elsewhere.
"The financial burden of maintaining the armed forces must be cut while cash must be freed for a powerful drive to develop the most promising technologies," Sergeyev told NTV television.

Boris Yeltsin sacked his predecessor last month for failing to make progress on the president's goal of a professional, non- conscript force by the turn of the century and for "whining" too often about the army's need for more money.

Chernomyrdin was quoted by Interfax news agency as saying the planned reforms were inextricably linked to the nation's finances: "That's essential, so that we don't get to the point where we take decisions and next day realise we have no funds."

His first deputy, economic reform chief Anatoly Chubais, heads a committee in charge of financing the modernisation of the vast, underfunded and demoralised Cold War-era army while Chernomyrdin himself heads a team looking at defence reforms.

There has been resistance from the high command to the civilian government's efforts to cut back, although Sergeyev, former head of the strategic missile command told Yeltsin earlier this month that reforms now had broad backing.

The head of the air force, General Pyotr Deinekin, was quoted by Interfax on Wednesday as saying its personnel would be cut by more than a third by 2001, in line with similar reductions across the board.

Deinekin also mentioned a scheme to cut the air force by 30,000 men a year until 2001. But an air force spokesman told Reuters the figures must be wrong as it would add up to cutting the corps, the elite of the Russian forces, by more than half.
The air force is due to expand technically from 150,000 to 184,000 after a planned merger with the air defence and anti-missile commands.
"The reduction is likely to start after the three merge into one," the air force spokesman said. "But slashing personnel by 90,000 in three years is a bit too much. It must be a mistake."

Sergeyev said last week he wanted to cut the fat from the armed forces administration -- the merger of the air forces is a case in point -- and to junk obsolescent hardware to invest in state-of-the-art equipment.
He said that by 1999 or 2000 there would be several new-look divisions in the army, reiterating his plan to set up flexible rapid-response units accross Russia.
Yeltsin has ordered Sergeyev to cut defence spending to 3.5 percent of gross domestic product by 2000 from five percent now.

A vote-grabbing move to end conscription by the same date, announced by Yeltsin during last year's election campaign, also stands, though it will be expensive and the deadline has been dropped from Kremlin statements on the subject.

Russia's armed forces are calculated at some 1.8 million men but even the generals concede they are not sure of their true size, making it hard to assess progress on previous plans to cut 200,000 men from the ranks this year.
